title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation fraud in which AI-generated content was used to fabricate a credible-seeming interview between two real, named public figures to promote a cryptocurrency platform. The failure is not a malfunction of a deployed product but a deliberate misuse of generative AI tools to produce disinformation at scale. The fabricated article sat within a wider infrastructure of fake reviews, fake news, and fake advertisements, all constructed to make an illegitimate investment opportunity appear legitimate.

The point of vulnerability is content distribution: the false material reached audiences through platforms that did not detect or remove it before victims could act on it. Catching this kind of fraud at the source would require detection of synthetic media before publication, which no platform appears to have done here. After publication it requires either automated scanning or human review, and ASIC's reported removal of tens of thousands of scams in a single year shows the volume makes both approaches difficult.

What is not established is the identity of the operators behind the Boulder Sparhaven platform, the number of people who lost money, or whether any enforcement action has resulted in findings against specific individuals or entities.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake online article claimed that Reserve Bank Governor Michele Bullock had a heated interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler about a cryptocurrency platform called Boulder Sparhaven. However, this interview never actually occurred. The article was part of a growing scam trend using artificial intelligence to create convincing fake content featuring well-known Australians to promote illegitimate investment opportunities. Australian Securities and Investments Commission research shows these deepfake scams are becoming increasingly sophisticated and prevalent.

ASIC removed 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase, with phishing scams up 279 percent and fake investment platforms up 151 percent. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is the most commonly impersonated person, followed by politicians and financial experts. Scammers build elaborate webs of deception using fake news articles, positive reviews, and advertisements to lure victims. ASIC urges consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers before investing, while presenter Kohler argues that platforms hosting this content should face heavy fines.
